LinkedIn:

I used to think I needed an elaborate system to manage screens at home-complex timers, app controls, lengthy negotiations. Then my husband and I started fighting about it daily, and our 2-year-old was picking up on every tense word.

Last month, we tried something radical instead: one simple routine.

Every evening after dinner (around 7pm), we sit together for exactly ten minutes. My daughter plays with blocks while we check if she needs anything before bedtime-a hug? A song? Water? After that quick connection, we do a two-part wind-down:

First, all devices get set aside. Not hidden-we're honest adults can be on phones during downtime-but active scrolling stops.

Second, we each share one thing from our day using three words maximum. That constraint keeps it light. Today mine were "meeting/stressed/tired."

The shift has been remarkable. We argue maybe once monthly now versus nightly. Our daughter goes to sleep calmer because she felt seen firsthand, not just managed through routines.

Turns out what kids actually need isn't more control over their media-they need us present for actual moments. Even messy ones.

What’s your family’s evening ritual?


Bluesky / X:

We stopped fighting about screen time when we started this 10-minute evening reset. Dinner → check-in with our toddler → both parents put phones down → everyone shares 3-word updates.

Night and day difference. Who else feels like evenings used to be battle mode?

If you’ve ever felt overwhelmed by the sheer amount of glowing screens in front of our kids today, please know I feel it too. It’s an emotional weight, trying to navigate what feels like a minefield of digital interactions for them. We are always learning how to teach genuine online caution without making them feel constantly monitored or stressed out. Because at the end of the day, we want them exploring freely, knowing they have tools to handle themselves.

When talking about online safety with my own 2-year-old, Maya, most discussions revolve around screen time limits or nap routines! But as she gets older, so do the threats. Lately, I’ve been focusing on teaching her-and keeping myself reminded-about digital pickpockets, which are basically scams that look super convincing until they ask for something sensitive, like a pjerkword or personal info.

One type of scam I keep hearing about involves fake school portals or educational games.
